title: Screen Bridge
user: Blind and low-vision computer users who need to operate a remote desktop, legacy program, or canvas-based app whose visual controls are missing from the accessibility tree.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker describes the limits of accessibility-API-based tools: they require app support and local installation, then asks about computer-vision accessibility software.
A developer documents an on-device camera/navigation companion for visually impaired users, showing current demand for private, browser-delivered perception aids.

recurrence: A direct 2025 request plus a 2026 independently built companion; inaccessible pixels remain a severe blocker when semantic APIs are absent.
current_workaround: Ask a sighted person, use brittle OCR, or abandon the task; conventional screen readers only expose declared semantics.
incumbents_and_gap: NVDA, VoiceOver, Windows Narrator, and Seeing AI are valuable, but none provides a tightly scoped, local desktop-region workflow that turns selected visual controls into keyboard-addressable labels without taking over the whole computer.
smallest_useful_product: A desktop companion that lets a user capture one screen region, runs local OCR and button/field detection, exposes numbered keyboard targets, and speaks confirmed text. Non-goals: autonomous computer control, face recognition, cloud screen streaming, or safety-critical navigation.
success_measure: In a 10-user assisted pilot, at least seven users complete one previously inaccessible visual-only dialog without sighted help.
monetization: freemium — a free local core earns trust; paid desktop capture integrations and support can fund maintenance.
constraints: Screen content can contain credentials and PII, so OCR/model inference must be on-device by default; clearly label uncertain detections; browser capture permissions limit coverage.
why_distinct: It is a user-invoked bridge for one inaccessible visual region, not a replacement screen reader or a generic AI vision chat wrapper.

title: Page Pointer
user: Parents, tutors, and emerging readers who want a non-distracting way to keep a child oriented to the exact word or line in a physical book.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A new parent explicitly wishes for a way to indicate the words being read to a child without having to point at every word.

The discussion of Braille Institute's updated Hyperlegible type includes readers using legibility-focused typography on e-readers, reinforcing demand for practical reading aids rather than decorative fonts.

recurrence: One explicit 2025 request and an independent 2025 reading-legibility discussion; losing place makes shared reading frustrating and interrupts comprehension.
current_workaround: A parent points with a finger, uses a bookmark or reading ruler, or buys a dedicated reading pen.
incumbents_and_gap: C-Pen and Scanmarker digitize or read text, while physical reading rulers are static. The missing lightweight option is a phone-only, temporary visual guide that follows a chosen line without recording the book.
smallest_useful_product: An offline mobile web app that uses the rear camera to detect printed text baselines, lets the adult tap the current word, and projects a high-contrast line/word guide on the phone screen. Non-goals: book scanning, child profiling, reading assessment, or cloud OCR archives.
success_measure: At least 60% of 20 family test sessions keep the guide active for ten minutes and parents report fewer than two manual re-orientations per page.
monetization: one-time — families should be able to use a privacy-preserving reading aid without a recurring charge.
constraints: Keep camera frames on device; support only printed Latin-script text in v1; avoid claims about diagnosing or treating dyslexia.
why_distinct: It supports joint attention during paper reading; it is neither an ebook reader nor a general OCR scanner.

title: Caption Clarity
user: People with high-frequency hearing loss who need captions styled around likely-to-be-misheard dialogue rather than one undifferentiated text stream.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker proposes bolding caption words likely to be misheard and allowing settings for different hearing-loss patterns.
A deaf commenter says automated captions are often only barely passable and can be miserable, despite being better than nothing.

recurrence: A direct 2025 feature request and an independent deaf user's account of unreliable captions; poor captions make dialogue comprehension exhausting.
current_workaround: Raise global caption size, rewind repeatedly, turn on subtitles that cannot be tailored, or use headphones.
incumbents_and_gap: Netflix, YouTube, Apple TV, and OS caption settings offer broad font controls, but do not give a personal, content-agnostic readability profile for user-provided WebVTT captions.
smallest_useful_product: A local WebVTT/SRT player and standards-compliant video overlay with profiles for emphasis, line length, pause-on-keyword, and user-defined confusing terms. Non-goals: scraping DRM services, speech recognition, or claiming audiological personalization.
success_measure: In a 30-minute comprehension test with supplied clips, profile users rewind at least 25% less than with ordinary captions.
monetization: one-time — the value is personal control over files the user already has, with no need to retain media.
constraints: No media hosting or DRM bypass; preserve copyright by accepting only local/user-authorized media; make all profiles adjustable rather than implying medical recommendations.
why_distinct: It improves how existing captions are consumed, not another automated-caption generator.

title: Caption Fix Queue
user: Small video teams and community educators who need to find the few caption defects that make an otherwise usable video inaccessible before publishing.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker reports spelling, grammar, punctuation, and transcription artifacts in major streaming captions and calls their neglect out directly.
A current workflow article treats caption generation as an automated upload step, highlighting why a lightweight human-review stage is still needed.

recurrence: Caption defects recur across large platforms and current creator automation; a single bad noun, negation, or timing error can alter meaning.
current_workaround: Manually read the entire SRT, trust automatic transcription, or send all caption work to an expensive external vendor.
incumbents_and_gap: Descript, Rev, YouTube Studio, and Premiere create/edit captions but make a full editing suite the unit of work. Small teams lack a local, prioritized review queue for existing VTT/SRT files.
smallest_useful_product: A local drag-and-drop SRT/VTT checker that flags improbable repeats, blank runs, unsupported characters, long reading-speed cues, inconsistent speaker names, and glossary mismatches; reviewers accept, dismiss, or repair each flag. Non-goals: generating captions, video hosting, or automatic factual correction.
success_measure: In pilots, reviewers resolve or dismiss 90% of flags in under ten minutes per ten-minute video and find at least one otherwise missed caption defect in 70% of files.
monetization: freemium — a free local checker invites adoption; shared glossaries and team review history can be paid.
constraints: All media/transcript parsing happens locally by default; flagging must be explainable and never silently rewrite a transcript; support caption standards accurately.
why_distinct: The product is a review prioritizer for captions already made, not a thin transcription-model wrapper.

title: Dialog Only Switch
user: Language learners and caption readers who need to toggle sound-effect descriptions separately from spoken dialogue when watching user-owned or classroom video.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An English learner asks why services offer only English closed captions with sound and music descriptions instead of dialog-only subtitles.
A current subtitling discussion highlights the multiple distinct needs subtitles must serve, reinforcing that one undifferentiated caption presentation does not fit every viewer.

recurrence: A direct streaming-service request and a separate text-first learning project point to a repeated mismatch between caption formats and learning needs.
current_workaround: Put up with noisy [MUSIC]/[DOOR SLAMS] cues, look for a separate subtitle track that often does not exist, or copy captions into a text editor.
incumbents_and_gap: Streaming services choose the caption tracks they expose; VLC can switch tracks but cannot intelligently filter one. There is no simple viewer that preserves timed dialogue while letting a learner hide non-dialogue cues on demand.
smallest_useful_product: An offline local-video/WebVTT viewer with a reversible dialogue-only filter, an always-visible transcript, and a one-key reveal of suppressed cues. Non-goals: altering third-party streams, removing accessibility tracks for others, or machine-generating dialogue labels without review.
success_measure: At least 70% of language-learner sessions use both filter states and users complete a selected dialogue exercise with fewer transcript pauses than in a standard player.
monetization: free — compatibility with user-owned classroom/media files is the adoption bottleneck; a free utility best serves it.
constraints: Accept only local or explicitly authorized media/captions; cue classification is user-editable and must never delete the original caption track.
why_distinct: It is a reversible caption-consumption mode, not a caption generator or a general video site.

title: Transcript Pocket
user: Deaf and hard-of-hearing podcast listeners who need a readable, synchronized transcript alongside audio files they already own.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker cannot find a way to embed captions in audio-only files and specifically notes the benefit for hard-of-hearing podcast listeners.
A current caption tool offers SRT/VTT output for uploaded audio, showing the common sidecar format exists even though podcast-player consumption remains weak.

recurrence: The original direct request remains relevant because current tools still center caption creation rather than comfortable playback of transcript sidecars.
current_workaround: Read an unsynchronized web transcript, use a video workaround with a static image, or avoid the episode.
incumbents_and_gap: Overcast, Pocket Casts, Spotify, and Apple Podcasts have inconsistent transcript support; generic media players rarely make local VTT/SRT sidecars first-class for audio files.
smallest_useful_product: An offline audio player that pairs a local MP3/M4A with VTT/SRT, follows and highlights the current phrase, supports large text/search/bookmarks, and exports a reading position. Non-goals: podcast-directory scraping, transcription, cloud sync, or hosting copyrighted audio.
success_measure: At least 50% of pilot listeners finish a 20-minute sidecar-captioned episode and use search or a bookmark at least once.
monetization: one-time — an offline player should remain usable indefinitely with a listener's own files.
constraints: Keep media local; robustly support common sidecar encodings and timestamps; do not imply a transcript is verbatim or provide medical accessibility certification.
why_distinct: It makes existing caption files usable with audio-only media instead of producing yet another transcript.

title: Color Context
user: People with color-vision deficiency who need to understand charts, status indicators, and marked-up documents when color alone carries important meaning.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker says OS and game color-correction settings do not cover the full spectrum of color blindness and asks technical users how they cope with screens.
The discussion covers renderer-level simulation of several color-vision deficiencies, illustrating that simulation exists while interpretation of a particular visual cue is still left to the user.

recurrence: A 2026 direct request identifies broad correction as insufficient; visual-only meaning creates ongoing errors rather than a one-time inconvenience.
current_workaround: Use OS color filters, ask a colleague, take a screenshot into a simulator, or avoid interfaces that rely on color.
incumbents_and_gap: macOS/Windows filters, Color Oracle, and Chrome DevTools simulate or shift palettes. They do not let a user click a sampled region and attach a durable personal label such as 'warning' or 'the red series' to a local image/PDF view.
smallest_useful_product: A local image/PDF viewer with sampled-color callouts, high-contrast texture overlays, user labels, and exportable annotated screenshots. Non-goals: diagnosing color vision, recoloring third-party live UIs, or claiming universal color correction.
success_measure: In a 15-user task set, participants correctly identify 90% of color-only legend/status meanings after annotating, versus their baseline task accuracy.
monetization: free — a small local accessibility utility benefits from frictionless availability and does not need user data.
constraints: No medical claims; annotations remain local unless explicitly exported; preserve the original image and disclose that overlays cannot recover missing semantic information.
why_distinct: It helps users record and recover the meaning of a specific cue, rather than merely simulating color blindness or applying a global tint.

title: Calm Scroll
user: People with vestibular disorders or screen-induced motion sickness who need a stable way to read ordinary web pages without parallax, auto-advance, or animated scrolling.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A current discussion of Android Motion Assist asks whether anti-nausea motion cues meaningfully reduce motion sickness, keeping visual-motion discomfort an active concern.
A first-person vestibular-disorder accessibility discussion prompted commenters to recognize an overlooked disability and the problem of motion-heavy modern web design.

recurrence: Current discussion of anti-nausea motion aids and first-person vestibular accounts connect visual motion to nausea, while page-level controls remain an afterthought.
current_workaround: Turn on OS reduced motion, disable a few site settings, use reader mode where available, or leave the page.
incumbents_and_gap: OS reduced-motion preferences and Safari/Firefox reader modes help unevenly; they do not give a user an inspectable, per-site motion budget that freezes individual offenders while retaining content and controls.
smallest_useful_product: A browser extension that detects autoplay, transforms, smooth-scroll, sticky animation, and parallax; offers a one-click stable reading mode plus per-site exceptions. Non-goals: rewriting site content, anti-ad blocking, or medical treatment claims.
success_measure: In a two-week pilot, users keep stable mode enabled on at least five sites and report a 50% reduction in sessions abandoned for visual discomfort.
monetization: one-time — per-browser local controls do not need an account or an ongoing service.
constraints: Respect browser extension permissions and CSP; do not break keyboard focus or media controls; describe comfort outcomes as user-reported, not clinical.
why_distinct: It provides targeted user control over real page motion instead of a generic dark theme or a site-wide accessibility audit.

title: Code Echo
user: Dyslexic developers and learners who need to inspect identifiers, punctuation-heavy syntax, and unfamiliar snippets without losing their place or relying on a generic screen reader mode.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A teacher asks dyslexic programmers which tools and learning techniques help, explicitly naming fonts, colors, and screen readers; replies emphasize autocomplete and spell checking over one-size-fits-all font claims.
A dyslexic developer describes the friction of learning new technology, a current account of reading-intensive developer workflows.

recurrence: A direct practitioner question and a 2026 first-person developer account show that technical reading, not programming ability, is the recurring barrier.
current_workaround: Turn on generic text-to-speech, magnify the IDE, copy snippets into another reader, or rely on autocomplete and spellcheck.
incumbents_and_gap: VS Code accessibility mode, screen readers, and OpenDyslexic-style fonts are broad tools. They do not offer an adjustable, code-aware pronunciation and chunk-replay layer for sighted readers who want selective support.
smallest_useful_product: A browser extension for documentation and code-review pages that reads a selected line/token with programmable punctuation and identifier pronunciation, shows one syntax chunk at a time, and offers a one-key replay history. Non-goals: IDE replacement, code generation, LLM explanations, or dyslexia diagnosis.
success_measure: At least 60% of pilot users complete an unfamiliar code-reading task with fewer rereads and voluntarily save three pronunciation/chunk preferences.
monetization: freemium — the core reader should be accessible; paid syncable language/pronunciation packs can support upkeep.
constraints: Never transmit code by default; use Web Speech only with clear browser/provider disclosure; users must control speech rate and all visual settings.
why_distinct: It is a deterministic, code-aware reading aid rather than a novelty font or an AI coding assistant.

title: Focus Resume Card
user: Developers with ADHD who need to resume an interrupted task from a small, concrete next action instead of rebuilding context from tabs, chat, and an open-ended task list.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The discussion frames types and other techniques as accessibility tools for the ADHD brain; a commenter describes daily mental schisms while programming.
A current first-person account says rigid focus systems failed for a distractible mind and argues for a flexible system that works with scattered attention.

recurrence: Independent 2025–2026 accounts describe persistent context-switching and rigid productivity tools failing the people they intend to help.
current_workaround: Keep many tabs open, write generic to-do items, re-read commits and chat after an interruption, or overbuild a personal planning system.
incumbents_and_gap: Notion, Todoist, Linear, and tab managers track work or tabs, but the next-resumption artifact is usually missing: a bounded snapshot tied to a specific page/file and a user-written next physical action.
smallest_useful_product: A local browser extension that makes a one-card checkpoint containing current URL, selected text, optional screenshot, elapsed focus block, and a required five-to-twelve-word next action; reopening presents only that card before tabs. Non-goals: task management, time surveillance, gamification, or LLM-generated plans.
success_measure: Over two weeks, at least half of pilot users resume 70% of saved cards within two minutes without reopening more than three unrelated tabs.
monetization: one-time — the personal local workflow should work without an account; optional encrypted sync can be later.
constraints: Store cards locally and allow redaction of page title/selection; never market as treatment; make all reminders opt-in and quiet by default.
why_distinct: It is an interruption-recovery primitive, not another backlog, Pomodoro timer, or AI productivity wrapper.

title: Eye Comfort Profiles
user: People with astigmatism, low vision, or reading fatigue who need a repeatable per-site reading layout rather than re-adjusting browser zoom and display settings every session.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A developer asks for ways to reduce eyestrain while coding with astigmatism and discusses the practical difficulty of using glasses and themes.
The 2025 Hyperlegible font discussion includes users choosing it for e-readers and debates legibility versus dyslexia-specific needs, showing that typography preferences are personal and contextual.

recurrence: A concrete eyestrain request and active 2025 typography discussion show that global font/theme choices do not fit every reader or source.
current_workaround: Change browser zoom, toggle a theme, use OS magnification, or accept unreadable line lengths and contrast on a site-by-site basis.
incumbents_and_gap: Browser zoom, reader modes, Stylus, and OS display options exist, but they are not a simple accessible profile system that consistently applies font, line length, spacing, contrast, and focus-line preferences to a chosen site or document type.
smallest_useful_product: A browser extension with named per-site profiles, a live readability preview, font fallbacks, line-width/spacing controls, and an optional reading focus band. Non-goals: vision testing, blue-light medical claims, or forcing a single dyslexia font.
success_measure: At least 70% of pilot users save three profiles and retain them after 14 days; users report fewer manual zoom/theme changes per reading session.
monetization: one-time — all meaningful layout control can run locally and should not require a subscription.
constraints: Never claim to treat eye conditions; preserve page semantics and keyboard navigation; do not collect browsing history beyond optional local profile matching.
why_distinct: It packages individualized, repeatable reading geometry rather than prescribing one font or replacing the browser reader mode.

title: Headset Cue Check
user: Screen-reader users and accessibility staff who need to evaluate whether a headset's speech, stereo, mono, and notification settings work for their own listening workflow before relying on it all day.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A developer responsible for accessibility software asks visually impaired HN users how they use headsets at home and work and what they would want in the future.
A current implementation account focuses on making text-to-speech reliable, confirming that audio accessibility quality depends on more than a device's basic channel test.

recurrence: There is a direct need to understand headset use in visually impaired workflows, while current text-to-speech implementation work shows that reliable audio behavior is still a practical concern.
current_workaround: Play arbitrary music, change OS settings by trial and error, or ask an accessibility specialist to set up and test a device.
incumbents_and_gap: Manufacturer audio tests and OS accessibility settings test channels or microphone in isolation. They do not provide a short, screen-reader-operable task sequence that checks practical speech intelligibility, interruption behavior, and personal cue preferences together.
smallest_useful_product: An offline accessible web test that runs labelled speech, stereo/mono, level, and interruption scenarios; records only user ratings and produces a local setup card with the exact OS settings to revisit. Non-goals: hearing tests, hardware certification, device telemetry, or diagnosis.
success_measure: In a 15-person pilot, 80% complete the task without sighted assistance and can reproduce their preferred headset setup on a second device using the setup card.
monetization: free — a neutral setup/check utility is more credible without headset affiliate incentives.
constraints: Must be fully keyboard and screen-reader operable; do not store ratings remotely; explicitly state that it is not an audiology test and browser audio routing is limited.
why_distinct: It evaluates a listener's end-to-end accessibility workflow, rather than being a generic sound test or another screen reader.
